item.title: 2nd Life Media AlamogordoTownNews.org and KALHRadio.org Release Free Nonpartisan Otero County Voter Guide for the Nov. 3 Election
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M., Oct. 20, 2026 — With early voting under way and Election Day two weeks off, 2nd Life Media has published the 2026 Otero County Nonpartisan Voter Guide, a free 32-page reference that walks voters through every contest and every question on the county’s Nov. 3 general-election ballot. The guide is a joint project of AlamogordoTownNews.org and KALHRadio.org, with New Mexico Conservative News and The 47th Voice as partners.

The guide is available now as a free pdf download at:

https://drive.google.com/file/d/15T7BLUbtTV_4abE6xiCmFr8K-FZF6U5W/view?…

Otero County voters will decide 33 separate items this year, from the U.S. Senate to the county probate judge, plus four proposed amendments to the New Mexico Constitution and three statewide bond questions. The guide organizes all of them in ballot order and, for every contested race, gives each candidate the same treatment: a background sketch, a summary of where the candidate stands in the candidate’s own words, and a section reporting what opponents and critics say. Each constitutional amendment and bond question gets a plain-English explanation, a side-by-side table of the arguments for and against, and a list of who is publicly supporting and opposing it.

“Every race. Every question. Both sides.” is the guide’s stated standard. The publishers do not endorse any candidate or ballot question in it. Candidate positions are drawn from the candidates’ own campaign materials, questionnaires, debates and interviews; criticisms are attributed to the opponents and organizations making them, so readers can judge the source for themselves.

What’s inside

• Federal: U.S. Senate (Ben Ray Luján vs. Larry Marker) and the 2nd Congressional District (Gabriel Vasquez vs. Greg Cunningham).

• Statewide: Governor and Lieutenant Governor (Haaland/Garcia Richard vs. Hull/Gallegos), Secretary of State, Attorney General, State Auditor, State Treasurer and Commissioner of Public Lands.

• Judicial: the Court of Appeals special election and yes/no retention votes on two Supreme Court justices, a Court of Appeals judge and two 12th Judicial District judges, with the Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission’s recommendation on each.

• Legislature: the Senate District 33 special election and House Districts 51, 53, 54 and 56.

• County: County Commission Districts 1 and 2, Sheriff, Assessor, Probate Judge, both Magistrate divisions and Public Education Commission District 7.

• Constitutional Amendments 1–4: ending the governor’s pocket veto, allowing school elections alongside partisan elections, nominating committees for university regents, and a salary for state legislators tied to median household income.

• Bond Questions 1–3: $393 million for senior centers, libraries and higher education — including $260,000 for Otero County senior-center vehicles and $1 million for NMSU-Alamogordo.

How, when and where to vote

The guide opens with a voting section built from the Otero County Clerk’s 2026 early-voting notice.

Early voting continues weekdays at the County Administration Building, 1101 New York Ave., Room 101, and Tuesday through Saturday at the Otero County Fairgrounds, 401 Fairgrounds Rd., through Saturday, Oct. 31

. One-day and short-run sites include Cloudcroft High School on Saturday, Oct. 24; the Inn of the Mountain Gods in Mescalero Oct. 28–30; and the Chaparral Far South Fire Station Oct. 29–31. T

oday, Oct. 20, is the last day to request an absentee ballot. 

On Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., and any registered Otero County voter may vote at any convenience center in the county. 

Same-day registration is available at every early-voting site and on Election Day for those who bring proof of identity and residency.

The guide also lists who is not on the ballot — candidates who filed but did not qualify, withdrew or were disqualified — so voters are not surprised by names they have seen on social media.

The guide was compiled Oct. 20, 2026, from the New Mexico Secretary of State, the Otero County Clerk, the Legislative Council Service, the Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission, candidate campaigns and statewide news coverage; a full source list appears on its final page. The guide may not be all comprehensive and any errors or omissions are accidential. The goal is to provide a non-partisan tool or summary of each issue and candidate. For the most up to date information contract the Otero County Clerks office or the SOS office.

item.title: A day after quitting the GOP, Zac Anaya says no one in either party is off limits
item.description:
RIO RANCHO — One day after announcing he had left the Republican Party, former GOP chair hopeful Zac Anaya said in a live interview Tuesday with Anthony Lucero that leaving the party has freed him to go after elected officials in both parties — including fellow conservatives he says he once went easy on.

"Independent doesn't mean I'm no longer a conservative," Anaya said. "It means that I'm able to vocalize my conservative values more than I would as a member of the Republican Party."

The 33-year-old Rio Rancho businessman announced Monday evening on social media that he had given up on the Republican Party of New Mexico and would register as an independent, 15 days before the Nov. 3 general election. In the live interview with host Anthony, he expanded on that post, took aim at party insiders over the governor's race and left the door open to returning — if the party changes its leadership.

In Monday's post, Anaya wrote that one of the most qualified Republicans to seek the governorship in a generation was struggling to raise money, without naming him. On Tuesday he named him: GOP nominee Gregg Hull, whom Anaya called "my mayor."

Anaya called Hull the most overqualified Republican gubernatorial candidate in at least 20 years and sharply criticized his Democratic opponent, Deb Haaland. He blamed Hull's fundraising gap on party insiders who he said resist Hull's "common sense ideas."

"They might do it on social media, but they're not doing it at a statewide monetary level," Anaya said of Republican support for Hull.

He went further, predicting Hull would lose by 11 points or more. "I hate to say that because I love Greg," he said.

The fundraising gap Anaya pointed to is real. Haaland remains well ahead in money according to reports filed Oct. 13. Hull raised about $634,000 in the latest period and roughly $1.5 million for the general election. His campaign has said the numbers reflect a focus on in-state donors — 99% of his donors are New Mexicans — and has cited donor fatigue after the June primary.

Anaya said that as an independent he would keep publishing political commentary and that officials of both parties are now fair game.

"If you're taking money, if you're married to a lobbyist, if you are making questionable votes, it's time to go after you," he said.

That line echoes his House District 60 primary campaign against state Rep. Joshua Hernandez (R-Rio Rancho), which Anaya lost in June. During that race Anaya filed a State Ethics Commission complaint accusing Hernandez of failing to disclose the lobbying clients of his partner and business associate; Hernandez called it a political stunt.

Anaya said Tuesday that Republican leaders, including Gail Armstrong and Rebecca Dow, called him during the primary and urged him to "leave Josh alone," and that he eased off as a result. He said Hernandez was one of five Republicans who voted for the universal child care bill, which Anaya later challenged in a lawsuit that the New Mexico Supreme Court rejected in July.

"That's not happening anymore," he said. "If you are corrupt, if you are making horrible votes, we're coming after you."

As 2nd Life Media reported Monday, Anaya's exit is the latest fallout from the yearlong fight over former party chair Amy Barela, who was removed by a court in May. Anaya briefly ran to replace her in June as part of the northern bloc opposing her, then stepped aside to avoid splitting that vote.

Anaya did not mention Barela by name Tuesday. But his conditions for coming back line up with the leadership question still hanging over the party, which enters the election under interim chair Mike Nelson and is set to pick a permanent chair after Nov. 3.

Anaya predicted a "reckoning" for Republicans after the election. "If the party can right itself with a proper chairperson and a new platform, then I may very well come back," he said.

Anaya said he left the Democratic Party after college because it had gone "a little wacko" and now sees Republicans doing the same — campaigning on conservative values and abandoning them in office. "At the end of the day, they love to spend our money," he said.

He described both parties as captured by their extremes, citing gender-related medical care for minors on the left and treating everything President Donald Trump says as "gospel truth" on the right. Most Americans, he said, sit somewhere in between.

He argued that Ronald Reagan and John F. Kennedy would both belong to the Forward Party today.

The host, KALHRadio.org’s Anthony Lucero for streaming Alamogordo Town News, compared Anaya's move to that of former Las Cruces Mayor Ken Miyagishima, who he said had voiced similar frustrations with the Democratic Party and endorsed Hull.

Anaya said he plans to spend more time with his wife, children and faith — a theme from Monday's post — while publishing opinion pieces on his website, zacanaya.com, and social media. 

He said he submits columns to newspapers across the state but that they have not run them. He has been extended an invitation to submit articles to us going forward. 

He closed by drawing on his recovery from addiction, which he has discussed publicly. 

"As somebody who is in recovery, I've learned that you have to admit the mistakes that you've made, admit that you're powerless, and surrender to a higher power," he said. "No politician is going to save you, no political party is going to save you."

item.title: Fact Check: John Block Sends Attack Letter: Relies on Insinuations and Falsehoods While Ignoring His Own Record of Division and Limited Results
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO  N.M. — In the closing weeks of the House District 51 campaign, Republican incumbent Rep. John Block mailed voters a two-page fundraising letter dated October 12, 2026. Rather than running primarily on a documented record of successful representation for Alamogordo and Otero County, the letter spends the bulk of its space attacking independent challenger Grace Nagamine with claims that public records, campaign finance filings, legislative documents, and her own disclosures contradict or leave without support

The letter portrays Nagamine as a Biden campaigner who “even met him,” a Harris supporter, a stand-in for an unnamed “far-left PAC” that has raised more than $300,000, an independent “the way Bernie Sanders is” who will caucus with Democrats the moment she reaches Santa Fe, and a “career criminal” whose record of “at least three felony convictions and other charges stretching over decades” disqualifies her

It contrasts this with Block’s assertion that he has delivered more than $11 million, kept promises on veterans and military families, and fought taxes and the shuttering of an ICE facility.

A review of New Mexico legislative records, Secretary of State campaign finance disclosures, court records, White House documents provided by the Nagamine campaign, and prior reporting shows the central attacks are unsupported or misleading. 

The letter also omits context that undercuts its framing, while overstating Block’s legislative achievements.

It arrives against a backdrop in which Block has faced public accusations from the state’s top election official of encouraging online harassment, maintains an active civil lawsuit set for trial after Election Day, and has used his own PAC structure in ways that route money involving his private company.

The “Career Criminal” Claim and the Record of Service

Block’s letter states that Nagamine’s record “includes at least three felony convictions and other charges stretching over decades for some of the most grievous crimes” and that this is “a career criminal’s record, not a public servant’s.”

According to Nagamine’s campaign and her published memoir, the convictions and related incarceration occurred in 2005–2008, tied to a period of domestic violence survival, addiction, and homelessness.

She has not disputed nor denied the existence of the record; she has described it publicly in her book The Grace Nagamine Story, in interviews, on social media, and as keynote speaker at a recent domestic violence survivors’ event.

Court-record reviews cited in local reporting have found no criminal cases against her in the roughly 18 years since.

The letter’s phrase “stretching over decades” does not match a record confined to a three-year period that ended nearly two decades ago.

The letter also omits the subsequent record of service.

White House letters provided by the Nagamine campaign document recognition under both parties through the President’s Volunteer Service Award program, which honors volunteer hours rather than political activity.

One letter signed by President Donald Trump congratulates her on the President’s Volunteer Service Award and thanks her for service to fellow Americans and those most in need.

A second letter signed by President Joe Biden presents the President’s Lifetime Achievement Award “in recognition of your 4,311 hours of service to this great Nation.” 

Nagamine has said that when she met Biden she brought her children so they could meet a sitting president, and that she would want them to show the same respect to any president regardless of party

Meeting a president and receiving volunteer recognition from two presidents is not campaigning nor politicking for either of them. 

The Block attack letter mentions the Biden meeting but not the Trump recognition.

Nagamine is a lifelong Alamogordo resident, former Mrs. New Mexico (2018–2019), founder of Royal Angels (a charity focused on children with special needs, established in honor of a granddaughter), a mother and grandmother, and an advocate for women, children, seniors, veterans, and survivors.

Her publicly stated platform centers on local issues including veterans and Holloman AFB, seniors and caregivers, children and CYFD reform, homelessness, and infrastructure. 

She has described running as a Decline to State (Independent) candidate because these problems do not belong to one party and has spoken of the need for bipartisan collaboration.

Unsupported Claims on Politics, Caucusing, and Outside Money

The letter calls Nagamine independent “the way Bernie Sanders is,” asserts she is “ready to caucus with” Democrats the moment she reaches Santa Fe, and claims she supported Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign.

It cites no statement from her pledging to caucus with Democrats, no public endorsement of Harris, and no donation record. 

Federal contributions are public via FEC filings; none supporting the Harris claim has been identified in available reporting.

Nagamine filed as a Decline to State candidate; her materials state she is not affiliated with any political party. No public record of a pledge to join the Democratic caucus nor any caucus has been located.

The letter further claims she is “backed by a far-left PAC that has raised over $300,000 and is now spending it to support Democrats down the ballot and flip our district blue.

It does not name the PAC. Nagamine’s state campaign finance reports through mid-2026 showed no PAC contributions of that scale. She has received a Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter endorsement based on her local knowledge and community work; an endorsement is not a $300,000 contribution. Available independent expenditures supporting her have been described as modest grassroots efforts. The claim lacks supporting documentation.

By contrast, Block’s own campaign reports list contributions from Chevron, Permian Resources, Devon Energy, and other corporate and out-of-district sources. Piñon PAC, of which Block is treasurer and which shares an address with his Piñon Post LLC, has raised tens of thousands of dollars, the large majority from Republican legislators outside Otero County. Filings show the PAC paid Piñon Post LLC more than $4,600 in 2026 with no purpose disclosed beyond generic descriptions such as “Check.” Money has also moved between Block’s campaign committee, the PAC, and Block personally.

Fact: The Block letter warns that “outside money does not knock on doors,” yet Block’s own filings show substantial outside support while local Otero County contributions to the PAC have been minimal.

Overstated Claims About Block’s Legislative Record

The letter credits Block with bringing home more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County. Every House member receives an equal share of capital outlay funds, roughly $2.5 million annually; four years of that standard allocation is approximately $10 million.

Local fact-checks have noted that Block voted against the 2026 capital outlay reauthorization and the state budget. In the 2026 session, four of the 37 measures he sponsored passed, and he was not the lead sponsor on any of them and ranks in the bottom 1/3 of his own Republican Caucus for effectiveness even surpassed by a first term novice Republican for effectiveness. 

He claims he “helped pass increased property tax relief for our veterans.” The veterans’ property-tax bills that became law (including HB 47 in 2025 and HB 285 in 2026) were sponsored by other legislators; HB 285 passed the House 67–0. He states he “passed bills to make it easier for military families.” He was one of five co-sponsors, not the lead sponsor, of HB 302 (2024), which added protections for military families.

He claims he fought “attempts to raise our taxes by trying to shutter our ICE detention facility.” HB 9 (2026) bars counties from ICE detention contracts, putting the Otero County Processing Center’s jobs and revenue at risk; it does not raise taxes, and lawmakers set aside funds to offset county losses

Fact: These claims range from inflated to partly true to misleading when measured against the legislative record.

Pattern of Division Versus Collaboration

While Nagamine has emphasized bipartisan approaches to local problems and has been recognized for service by presidents of both parties, Block’s public record includes sharp partisan attacks.

In November 2024, New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver publicly accused Block of encouraging or “egging on” online harassment and threats she received after the election, including during a legislative committee hearing.

She indicated she planned to file a police report related to intimidation of election officials. Block denied threatening or harassing her, offered a qualified apology for any violent threats directed at her, and characterized questions about her policy positions as legitimate debate.  The episode is documented in contemporaneous reporting by the Albuquerque Journal, Santa Fe New Mexican, and Associated Press.

Block has also been a frequent critic of Democratic leadership, including filing ethics complaints and using his Piñon Post platform for pointed commentary.

Separately, he is a defendant in an ongoing LBGTQ civil lawsuit filed by his former domestic partner, over a property agreement; a judge has set the case for a multi-day trial beginning in March 2027. 

Block threatened a defamation lawsuit and previously told constituents the matter had been resolved amicably; court orders show it was not. A State Ethics Commission complaint involving related matters was also filed against him. .

New Mexico law requires clear disclaimers on campaign advertising identifying who authorized and paid for it. The letter reviewed carries Block’s campaign branding and lists an address for checks but does not display a boxed statement of authorization and payment of the campaign materials in the manner described under state statute and rules. Whether that complies is a question for the State Ethics Commission and the SOS of which is investigating. 

Conclusion

Block’s letter asks voters to judge character and trust “neighbors.

On the claims that can be checked against public records, Nagamine’s history of service is documented by volunteer awards from both President Trump and President Biden.

Her criminal record is real, old, self-disclosed, and followed by years of clean time and community work.

The letter’s characterizations of her politics, funding, and caucus intentions lack supporting evidence.

Block’s own claims about delivering uniquely for the district are inflated relative to the shared capital outlay process and the legislative record of co-sponsorship rather than sole authorship.

The Block letter continues a pattern of attacking an opponent through insinuation rather than resting the case primarily on a clear, unvarnished record of results for District 51.

item.title: Guest Commentary: which candidate has best demonstrated honesty and trustworthiness, the values you want representing your interests? by Marty McFarland
item.description:
John Block’s most recent campaign letter asserts that “…a public servant should be someone neighbors can trust,” after which he goes on to push, once again, the narrative of his opponent’s criminal history.

Grace Nagamine has not denied her past. She has spoken freely and honestly about her history and how that has shaped her views and made her into the advocate she is for the disenfranchised.

Contrast that to the numerous posts by Block that have recently come to light, in which he mocks local protesters who are actually the constituents he purports to represent. Or the recent posts in which he makes racist and disparaging comments about Deb Haaland and Sen. Elizabeth Warren. Posts he has since taken down. Of course, nothing really disappears from the internet.

Getting back to the question Block raises in his recent campaign plea for money and votes: which candidate has best demonstrated honesty and trustworthiness, the values you want representing your interests?

Marty McFarland

item.title: 'Easy to be a Monday morning quarterback': Dr Hernandez answers critics of city projects
item.description:
Alamogordo NM -Alamogordo's former interim city manager Dr Stephanie Hernandez is pushing back against recent criticism of four city infrastructure projects, arguing that critics are judging past decisions without knowing the circumstances behind them.

"It's easy to be a Monday morning quarterback," Hernandez said in recorded remarks. "I worked under city managers, and I would never criticize the decisions because I don't know all the circumstances they faced."

The four projects — the Oregon Avenue project, the Great Blocks New York Ave he project, the fire station and the 10th Street Bridge — were recently criticized during a public meeting. Hernandez said three of them dated back to 2022, under former City Manager Brian Cesar. Since then, the city's top administrative job passed from Cesar to Hernandez, to Rick Holden, and back to Hernandez.

"These projects were already designed," she said. "Much of the funding came from grants with deadlines. Further delays risk the projects altogether."

Hear in her own words:

Hernandez said the Great Blocks project was backed by millions of dollars in state money and went through three change orders, including a pedestrian improvement added in response to public feedback that fell "completely outside the original scope." She noted the project later received an award from the state and she as also recognized by the state for excellence in collaborations with the State MainStreet organization.

The fire station, she said, went through three fire chiefs and several changes. Chief Ramirez wanted the project's funding used to improve response times on the city's south side, and the city got that funding reauthorized.

On Oregon Avenue, Hernandez said new infrastructure that was not part of the original design was added so the street would not have to be torn up later. The commission approved two change orders on that project. Hernandez said she questioned a later extension, but it "was approved without much discussion."

The 10th Street Bridge was found to have structural problems, and a permanent fix required more engineering, time and money, she said. Hernandez said Commissioners Rardin and Guthrie pushed hard to reopen the street without a permanent solution, while Hernandez and Rardin criticized the inconvenience. Staff worked on another temporary fix while designing a longer-term Washington canal project, with 10th Street as its first phase.

Hernandez said the four projects did not reflect the city's full record. About 20 other projects were completed, she said, including the Hubbard Bridge — a problem she remembered from childhood — which was finished in roughly three months.

She said several other projects have completed designs from the same engineering firms whose work is now being re-reviewed, and that she tracked every project and still has records showing where each stood when she left. Projects such as Oregon WSRP phases two and three should be moving forward, she said. She had wanted one underway during the summer to minimize disruption around the school administration building, and the Alaska section finished before Christmas because of increased traffic to the post office.

But knowing she was leaving, Hernandez said, she chose not to start those projects. "I respected the incoming city manager enough not to start projects and tie his hands."

Hernandez acknowledged she was not satisfied with how every project was handled. She said she was vocal about contractor delays, which at times put her at odds with contractors and commissioners, and that the city was already working toward better, fairer processes.

"There's a difference between improving and waiting for perfection," she said. "Anyone who's remodeled a home with the best plans and contractors knows that problems are going to happen. You address them and move on."

She warned against letting projects sit while funding opportunities expire.

"Citizens don't benefit from projects sitting on paper; they benefit when projects get completed," Hernandez said. "And Alamogordo deserves progress."

item.title: Presumptive Sheriff Elect Geraldine Yazza Martinez Shares Halloween Safety Tips
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — With Halloween just around the corner, Geraldine Yazza Martinez, the Republican candidate for Otero County Sheriff, is reminding families to keep safety in mind as trick-or-treaters head out across the county.

In her own words:

In a message to the community, Martinez addressed "all the little goblins, ghouls, princesses, superheroes, and accompanying adults" who will be out knocking on doors and traveling through neighborhoods on Halloween night.

Her first piece of advice was aimed at parents: "Adults, supervise your kids." For older children going out without parents, she recommended the buddy system and carrying a flashlight.

Martinez urged trick-or-treaters to use sidewalks or paths and to cross only at corners and designated crosswalks. She also stressed making eye contact with drivers before stepping into the road, "that you know they see you."

For motorists, her message was to slow down and stay extra alert in residential areas. She asked drivers to put away cell phones, turn on their headlights, and use caution around driveways and alleys.

"As always, and most importantly, stay sober," Martinez said. "No drinking and driving."

She closed on a lighter note, telling kids not to eat too much candy — "at least not until your parents have had a chance to check it out first."

"We want everyone to have a fun, safe Halloween," she said.

item.title: Tularosa trustees delay vote on 190-foot cell tower after residents pack hearing
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Board of Trustees heard more than an hour of testimony Monday on a proposed 190-foot cell tower at 44 Sunset Road, and then put off its decision. Most of the testimony came from residents who oppose the project. The board will vote at a special meeting that has not been scheduled yet.

"I don't like to make this like quick decision," the mayor said at the end of the Oct. 19 special meeting. "I want to look at everything, look it over, take considerations in before we make that quick decision." The trustees agreed.

The village attorney, speaking by phone, told the board the item had been noticed properly and it could have acted that night. She also said the vote could not go on the board's regular meeting this Wednesday because there was not enough time to put it on the agenda.

The application

Flagship One LLC is asking for a special use permit, case 2026 SUP 002, to build a wireless tower on a parcel of about 15 acres behind a home. The applicant's representative, Sean Milks, said the parcel needed its own address for the tower. The hearing was quasi-judicial, which means trustees were reviewing the record built by the Planning and Zoning Commission. That commission adopted findings of fact on Sept. 8.

Shannon Naysenzer of Planning and Zoning told the board the commission does not recommend approval or denial of special use permits. It does recommend 12 conditions that Flagship One would have to meet before getting a building permit. They include:

Flagship One has also agreed to reserve a spot on the tower, at 150 feet or lower, for village and emergency equipment at nominal cost.

Milks joined by phone after about 15 minutes of audio problems. He said the company now proposes a monopole instead of a three-legged lattice tower. A monopole is 70% to 75% smaller in diameter and costs more to build, he said. He also said it is designed to fold onto itself in sections instead of falling over, and that it will not carry a light.

"I know we upset people from time to time," Milks said. "We're trying to do a happy medium, which is another reason I opted to offer to make the [pole] significantly smaller."

He said his company has built 46 sites in New Mexico, and 30 to 35 of them sit close to homes. He said he had never seen or heard of a tower falling in the state in his 29 years in the business.

Setbacks dispute

The sharpest exchanges were about the fall zone. Eva J. Gonzalez asked whether the tower meets the setback, the tower's height plus 10%, on all four sides of the property. Milks said it meets three. In cases like this, he said, the company submits an extra analysis from a New Mexico licensed engineer certifying that the pole and foundation are over-engineered.

"I'm telling you under oath, the pole will not fall down," Milks said.

"And I'm telling you under oath that you cannot guarantee anything like that," Gonzalez replied.

David Gonzalez, of Cortez Drive, said county assessor records put the parcel at 362 feet wide. By his math, a 190-foot tower plus 10 feet on each side would need 400. He also said the application includes drawings dated August 2018 that refer to Raglan, New Mexico. He listed five different tower heights in the paperwork, up to 203 feet, and said the federal antenna registration still describes a lattice tower. "Why are we even looking at this application if all this information is wrong?" he asked. The mayor ended his comments when his five minutes ran out.

Naysenzer said the main application does list Tularosa and that the permit is preliminary. The village attorney said the commission's findings clearly describe a 190-foot tower with a one-to-one fall zone. She added that trustees could make the monopole design a condition of approval.

Coverage, petition and alternatives

Eva Gonzalez cited CarrierLytics, an analytics platform that uses FCC coverage maps. It shows T-Mobile coverage at 98.6% and Verizon at 98.3% in the 88352 ZIP code. "There is no significant gap in coverage warranting the installation of another cell tower in the village," she said. She then submitted a petition with 198 signatures from Tularosa residents asking the board to deny the permit. Milks answered that capacity, not just coverage, is driving new sites, and that the carriers have signed a 30-year lease.

Several speakers suggested other sites. Frank Portillo said a landowner east of the site has a small range of hills that could hold a shorter tower out of residents' direct view, and wants to talk with the company. Milks said the project had already gone too far through surveys and reviews to start over. Kevin Ferguson asked about land the village plans to buy. The mayor said the village cannot offer land it does not own yet.

Billy Hobson questioned whether a personal relationship with the property owner influenced where the tower would go. Milks said the site was chosen from a search area set by a radio-frequency engineer.

Other residents talked about Tularosa's place on the National Register of Historic Places, their mountain views and home values. "We don't have high rises. We don't have skyscrapers. We don't need a cell phone tower here," said Denise Ottaviano, whose mother lives on Cortez Drive. Juan A. Osorio raised health concerns. Before testimony began, the mayor had reminded the audience that the federal Telecommunications Act of 1996 bars local governments from denying a tower over radio-frequency health concerns if it meets FCC standards.

Larry Berry asked what happens to the removal bond if the company goes bankrupt. Milks said FCC rules require the owner to take the tower down if no carrier broadcasts from it for six straight months. He said the bond is paid up front and stays tied to the tower.

Village staff said they sent 49 certified notices to nearby property owners, reaching farther than the required distance. Six were not picked up.

item.title: Judge Orders Meta to Pay $25 Billion in New Mexico Deception Case
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms Inc. to pay a $25 billion civil penalty, concluding that the company formerly known as Facebook spent more than a decade misleading the public about how it handled users' data, policed misinformation and hate speech, and enforced its own rules.

First Judicial District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew found that the state was entitled to $219.5 billion under the maximum penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act — $5,000 for each of 43,899,720 violations found by a jury — before reducing the award to $25 billion. The judgment, filed at 10:51 a.m., also orders interest to accrue at 15% a year until the penalty is paid in full. At that rate, interest alone would amount to roughly $3.75 billion a year.

The order does not explain how the court arrived at the $25 billion figure. The judge reserved a decision on injunctive relief, which could require changes to Meta's practices, pending further briefing.

The case, State of New Mexico ex rel. Raúl Torrez v. Meta Platforms, Inc., was filed in 2021 and decided after a 13-day trial before a 12-person jury.

Jurors found 26 public statements by Facebook and its executives to be unlawful and willful. The statements were made between May 24, 2010, and Aug. 18, 2021, through Facebook's own newsroom, earnings calls, national television and print interviews, and public conferences. Some were made personally by CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former COO Sheryl Sandberg.

The statements fell into five areas:

The violation counts came from the jury's estimate of each statement's audience in New Mexico. For each statement, jurors used either 1,386,648 — Facebook's New Mexico monthly active users as of mid-2020 — or 2,100,000, roughly the state's entire population. The jury also found five separate willful violations for unconscionable trade practices, one in each subject area.

Much of the judgment focuses on what Facebook said after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke in March 2018. The company publicly pledged to investigate every app with large-scale access to user data, audit suspicious apps, ban developers who misused data, make sure improperly obtained data was deleted, and notify every affected user.

The court found Facebook knew at the time it could not keep those promises because of poor record-keeping and lax vetting of developers. Over the three-year investigation, the company conducted only 14 forensic "audits," despite thousands of apps showing suspicious activity. It notified users about just two apps, after deliberately narrowing its internal definition of "misuse" to limit the burden of notification, the judge wrote.

Facebook linked 1,585 of the more than 2,000 problem apps identified at trial to New Mexico accounts, affecting at least 1,146,225 state residents — more than 80% of its New Mexico users. The investigation ended in March 2021 without a public announcement, even though an internal legal review in September 2019 concluded the company could not say it had met its commitments.

The judge also cited a Sandberg email sent to advisers shortly after the scandal broke, warning that a "MILLION developers" had access to the data.

The court separately found that, more than a year before Facebook announced in 2014 that it was ending "friend sharing," the company was already planning undisclosed exemptions for favored business partners.

The judgment quotes a private Zuckerberg email in which he wrote that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings," and outlined a plan to make more information public without encouraging users to change their settings. The court found Zuckerberg chose to exploit that confusion to help Facebook compete with Twitter.

On content moderation, the court found that Facebook's internal research showed its systems recommended groups and pages containing known misinformation, and that its "CrossCheck" program let content from celebrities, business partners and other high-profile accounts stay up while under extended review — about 12 days on average for U.S. accounts, according to the Oversight Board. The judge quoted a 2020 document in which integrity chief Guy Rosen acknowledged that the company was effectively delaying enforcement against violating content from those accounts.

Judge Mathew wrote that the number of violations, their duration, the involvement of senior leadership and the "clearly intentional and systematic" nature of the conduct supported the highest penalty allowed under state law.

The court rejected Meta's argument that its $5 billion settlement with the Federal Trade Commission should weigh against a large penalty, finding that prior penalties and consent decrees "have not deterred Meta." It also noted that the U.S. Supreme Court has not held that the Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive fines applies to corporations.

The judgment cites Meta's 2025 annual report, which listed revenue of nearly $201 billion and stockholders' equity of about $217 billion. The $25 billion penalty equals roughly one-eighth of a year's revenue.

This is Meta's second major trial loss in Santa Fe this year. In March, a separate jury in a 2023 lawsuit brought by Attorney General Raúl Torrez ordered Meta to pay $375 million after finding the company misled the public about child safety on Facebook and Instagram. Meta said it would appeal that verdict.

Meta's response to Wednesday's judgment was not immediately available.

item.title: Save the Date: Emo Takes the Stage: Rebel Performing Arts Presents 'Sugar, We're Goin' Emo'
item.description:
Alamogordo NM- For anyone who once wore black eyeliner to homeroom, mouthed every word of a breakup song in the car, or found comfort in a band that seemed to understand exactly how they felt, Rebel Performing Arts has a show for you coming to Otero Arts in the cultural Arts District at 12th Street and Indiana. 

Sugar, We're Goin' Emo, a new musical revue celebrating the music and memories of the emo era, opens Friday, Nov. 13, at Otero Artspace, 1118 Indiana Ave. in Alamogordo. The production brings together a cast of local performers and a live band for a night that moves from vulnerable ballads to explosive, sing-along anthems — the kind of music that defined a generation raised on bands like My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy and Paramore.

The show is co-directed by husband-and-wife team Andy and Amy Bethard, who describe the production as a collision of their two worlds.

"Andy is the quintessential emo kid, and I'm the theatre kid," Amy Bethard said. "We've been together for 17 years, and our shared love of emo music is part of our story. This show combines his love for the music with my love for theatrical storytelling."

The result, she said, is a production that treats the genre with the seriousness its fans have always felt it deserved.

Rebel Performing Arts, which has also performed under the name Rebel Music Theatre, is one of Alamogordo's newest theater groups. It was founded in 2025 by local theater veterans Rosemary "Rosie" Daffern, Jordynn Marelich and Tabitha Plante, with a mission to empower performers, encourage conversations about mental health through the arts, and broaden the city's creative offerings.

The company debuted with A Night of Broadway Revue, then returned to Otero Artspace in September 2025 with Decades in Harmony, a revue of songs that shaped generations. At the time, 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News described the group as part of a growing arts corridor around Otero Artspace near 12th Street and Indiana Avenue, just blocks from the revitalization of New York Avenue's 1100 and 1200 blocks. This past May, the company staged The Aux Chronicles, a revue built around the hits that defined a decade and featuring performers from several generations.

Sugar, We're Goin' Emo is the latest in that string of revues, and its focus on vulnerability and feeling understood fits squarely within the company's mental-health mission.

Emo has long been the punchline of jokes about angsty teenagers, and Bethard said one of her goals was to push back on the idea that it's just noise.

"Beneath the guitars and screaming vocals are powerful stories about love, heartbreak, identity, belonging and growing up," she said. "Emo music was never 'just a phase.' It's storytelling. It's vulnerability. It's finding comfort in knowing someone else has felt the same things you have."

That emotional honesty, she said, is a natural fit for the stage. "When you combine that with the energy and creativity of theatre, you get something truly special. I truly believe there's an emo song for everyone."

Beyond the nostalgia, the production is a showcase for local talent. Jonece Tallant serves as producer and Jordynn Marelich as music director, with Bradley Oliver and Rosie Daffern as choreographers. Marelich and Daffern are both co-founders of the company.

This time the music will be performed by a live band, led by Corey Shumard, something the directors say they are especially excited about. Like the company's earlier shows, the revue strings songs together rather than following a single plot, moving through the genre's full emotional range from quiet, confessional ballads to loud, fast anthems made for singing along.

"This production highlights the creativity and passion of local performers coming together to celebrate a genre that means so much to so many people," Bethard said.

We will be doing a followup story with cast notes and photos and more stay turned but until then purchase your tickets these shows sell out fast!

item.title: In Memory of Henry E. Garcia
item.description:
Henry E. Garcia (My Pa, My Pop), passed peacefully surrounded by his family at home in Alamogordo on Sunday, October 18th, 2026. He was born on September 2nd, 1933 in Roswell.

He is survived by his loving wife of 65 years, Bertha Garcia. And his pride and joy, Carlos and Tina, his children. He is also survived by his sister, Frances Fierro and brother, Orlando Garcia.

He is preceded in death by his parents, Pedro and Josephine Garcia; his brothers, Roque, Richard, and David; and his sisters, Juanita and Adella.

He was a Navy Veteran who served aboard the USS St. Paul and the USS Frank E. Evans in the aftermath of the Korean conflict.

He was a man of few words, a funny guy, and his heart was full of love for his friends and family!

Rosary to be done at Scenic Chapel Tuesday, October 27th from 6 to 7 pm.

item.title: Meet Troy Stegner: Bringing a New Voice to Pop Culture to Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org
item.description:
Hey, fellow nerds! I'm Troy Stegner, owner of Zia Comics and the owner/promoter of El Paso Comic Con. I'm excited to introduce myself as a new article provider for the Pop Culture category.

If there's one thing I've learned in my journey through nerdom, it's that being a fan of something is more than just a hobby. It's a way to connect with people, build friendships, discover new interests, and find a community that shares your passions. It doesn’t matter if you're into comics, anime, video games, tabletop gaming, collectibles, movies, television, or anything else in the wonderfully weird world of fandom, you're among friends here. And remember, you don’t have to be a hardcore pro in your fandom. Casual fandom is cool too!

A Little About Me

My journey in pop culture has been built around a simple idea: everyone is a fan of something, and those interests deserve a place to thrive.

As the owner of Zia Comics, with locations in Las Cruces and Alamogordo, New Mexico, I've dedicated myself to creating a destination where fans can explore their interests, discover new favorites, and connect with others who share their enthusiasm. Zia is about much more than comic books. Pop culture casts a long shadow and many things fall under that umbrella. Our goal is to help people find the things that make them happy or to discover their next obsession.

I'm also the owner behind El Paso Comic Con, an event that brings fans, creators, celebrities, artists, vendors, and communities together to celebrate the things they love. Through these businesses, I've had the opportunity to see firsthand how powerful fandom can be. It brings generations together, gives people common ground, supports creative talent, and creates memories that last long after the convention floor closes.

What Can You Expect From My Articles?

As a new contributor to the Pop Culture category, I want to cover the topics fans are interested in, not just the stories everyone is already talking about. Expect a mix of pop culture news, industry insights, gaming discussions, comic and manga spotlights, convention culture, collecting, fandom trends, and behind-the-scenes perspectives from someone who works in this world every day.

I'll also be drawing on my experiences as a retailer and convention organizer to explore some of the bigger questions facing pop culture. What's happening in the comic book industry? Why do certain franchises stand the test of time? What makes a great convention experience? Which games deserve more attention? And what does the future of fandom look like?

Of course, pop culture is enormous, and there's no way one person can cover everything. That's why I want this to be a conversation rather than a one-way broadcast.

What Nerdy Topic Should I Cover First?

Here's where you come in.

What do you want to read about? Are you curious about how comic shops operate behind the scenes? Want to learn more about the business of comic cons? Interested in the latest gaming trends, hidden gems in anime, the world of collectibles, or the history behind your favorite franchises?

Maybe you've got a question about something in the nerd world that you've always wanted answered. Maybe there's a topic that doesn't get enough attention. Or maybe you just want someone to dig deeper into a particular fandom. Let me know.

Drop your suggestions in the comments. Tell me what you’d like to see more information about. Your suggestion might become one of my next articles.

I'm excited to be part of this community and look forward to exploring the wonderful world of pop culture with all of you.

Until next time, don’t be afraid to celebrate your fandom, no matter how nerdy it might be. Never be embarassed about the things you love.

Fly Your Nerd Flay High!

Troy Stegner
Owner, Zia Comics | El Paso Comic Con

item.title: Regulators move PNM billing probe forward; final order due Nov. 5
item.description:
LAS CRUCES — The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission on Thursday unanimously moved ahead with a formal investigation into Public Service Company of New Mexico's estimated and delayed electric bills this summer, sending the order that would authorize the probe back for revisions before a final vote at its Nov. 5 meeting.

The item — Case No. 26-0000176, a petition from the commission's own Public Interest Advocacy Staff — came up during the PRC's Oct. 22 regular open meeting at Guthrie Hall on the New Mexico State University campus.

Rather than simply approving or denying the draft order, the three commissioners voted to rework its language so investigators have clearer direction on how far the probe should reach.

Nibert said the agency needed to show residents of the two counties that "we're concerned about their particular plight." He added that while the problem surfaced in those counties, staff remain free to determine whether it occurred elsewhere, and said he hoped the issue was not widespread but wanted the investigation to find out.

Commissioners also noted that although Otero and Lincoln county customers make up only about 5 percent of PNM's customer base, residents there have no alternative provider for electric service.

Customers in the Alamogordo area began complaining in July that PNM was estimating their usage instead of reading meters, a problem the utility attributed largely to a shortage of meter readers. The mayor encouraged PNM to host meetings and listening sessions due to concerns being raised. Independent New Mexico House Rep District 51 Candidate pushed a call to hear from constituents and attended meetings to give constituents answers. 
A group was formed and organized PNM Customers United. The Mayor of Alamogordo, Sharon McDonald, pushed for local public dialogue and hosted a PRC discussion and a PRC town hall in Alamogordo on Sept. 29. At that event some residents said monthly bills that normally ran $150 to $200 had jumped as high as $1,700, according to the staff filing.

PNM issued 28,472 estimated bills in August alone — about 5.5 percent of the bills it scheduled that month — and the shortage spread beyond southern New Mexico to other parts of its service area.

PRC staff filed their petition in early October asking the commission to authorize a formal investigation, independent testing of a sample of meters in Alamogordo and Ruidoso, monthly status reports and a final public report. Staff proposed that PNM pay for the meter testing and that the sample be chosen with help from PNM Customers United, a grassroots group that attended the Alamogordo town hall. The petition said the affected communities "deserve a full accounting."

Staff said they intend to start with four questions:

The state Department of Justice also pressed PNM over the high bills last month, hand-delivering a letter to PNM President and CEO Don Tarry.

PNM spokesperson Eric Chavez said the company understands customers' concerns, remains committed to supporting those affected, and will fully cooperate with the investigation, including providing information on what happened, how customers were affected and what the utility has done in response.

PNM Customers United, which formed in August and says it now has more than 2,100 members on Facebook, brought the four investigation questions to regulators at the Alamogordo town hall.

"This is great news for Otero and Lincoln counties," said Rebekah Garcia Stewart Thorp, an advocate with the group who spoke at Thursday's meeting. "We won't stop until there is an acceptable resolution on this issue," she added.

According to the group, once the final order is approved, PRC staff will have 120 days to complete their investigation and prepare a report.

The commission is expected to take up the final wording of the order at its next regular open meeting, Thursday, Nov. 5, at 10 a.m. in Room 309 of the State Capitol in Santa Fe. The meeting is open to the public in person and will be livestreamed on YouTube; public comment sign-up is through public.comment@prc.nm.gov or 505-490-7910.

Customers with billing concerns are advised to contact PNM first. Unresolved complaints can be filed with the PRC's Consumer Relations Division at 1-888-427-5772 or online at prc.nm.gov.

item.title: Tigers Roll Past Deming 49-7 for Tiger Senior Family Night
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — On a night set aside to honor its seniors and their families, the Alamogordo Tigers gave them plenty to cheer about.

Alamogordo scored four touchdowns in the first quarter and rolled to a 49-7 district win over Deming on Thursday at Tiger Stadium and Bob Sepulveda Track and Field at Alamogordo High School. The victory improves the Tigers to 5-4 overall and 4-2 in district play heading into the final week of the regular season.

Senior family night drew Tiger fans into the stands in black and gold, with splashes of pink throughout the crowd, on the sideline and on the field. Players wore pink sleeves and cheerleaders wore pink shirts and hair bows as the community turned out to celebrate the class of seniors playing their final regular-season home game

The Tigers wasted little time making it a memorable evening. Quarterback Nathanael Cereceres hit Tristan Bowman on a 70-yard touchdown pass with 11:42 left in the first quarter, and Russell's extra point made it 7-0.

Bowman found the end zone again at the 7:27 mark, this time on a 5-yard run, to push the lead to 14-0. Jayden Valdez followed with a 1-yard touchdown run with 3:10 left in the quarter. Cereceres then took matters into his own hands, scoring on a 5-yard run with 1:02 remaining. By the end of the first quarter, Alamogordo led 28-0.

The Alamogordo defense kept Deming off the board through the second quarter, and the offense added one more score before the break. Qymani Patterson ran in from 5 yards out with 1:37 left in the half. Deming blocked the extra point, but the Tigers carried a commanding 34-0 lead into the locker room.

Halftime brought one of the night's highlights, as the Alamogordo High School marching band took the field with an outer-space themed show. The performance featured a flying-saucer prop with a green alien, three large purple backdrops of futuristic cityscapes and color guard members dressed as aliens in green costumes and antennae. Seniors in the band wore pink sashes as part of the evening's recognition

The Tigers picked up where they left off in the third quarter. Rudy Wolfe threw a 2-yard touchdown pass to Sean Piper with 9:00 on the clock, and Russell's kick made it 41-0. The score held through the end of the quarter.

Alamogordo's defense carried its shutout deep into the fourth quarter. The scoreboard still read 41-0 with 3:09 to play before Deming finally broke through. Richard Holguin connected with Jordan Milo on a 35-yard touchdown pass in the closing minute to get the Wildcats on the board

The Tigers answered on the very next play. Tanner Nowaczck (featured above with family) fielded the kickoff and raced 85 yards for a touchdown with six seconds left, and Russell added the extra point to seal the 49-7 final.

Russell handled kicking duties throughout the night, converting six extra points. Cereceres accounted for two touchdowns, one passing and one rushing, and Bowman scored twice, once as a receiver and once as a runner.

After the final whistle, Tiger players gathered in front of the student section and raised their helmets toward the stands. Seniors then joined their families on the track for photos, wrapping up a night that celebrated both a dominant win and the players who have given years to the program.

Alamogordo closes out the regular season next Friday, Oct. 30, on the road at Chaparral.

item.title: Small Business Spotlight: Oppenheimer Gasthaus Brings a Taste of Germany to Downtown Alamogordo
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Downtown Alamogordo has a new favorite place to slow down. Oppenheimer Gasthaus, at 902 New York Avenue on the corner of 9th Street, serves scratch-made German food, imported German beer on draft, and old-world hospitality in the heart of the historic New York Avenue Business and Cultural Arts District.

The restaurant celebrated its grand opening this spring, and the community showed up in force. And a few weeks back it celebrated its first Octoberfest with a message to customers, the Gasthaus team thans locals for turning out and showing them "lots of love.”

In German, a Gasthaus (pronounced "gahst-house") is a guest house: a cozy, often family-run inn or tavern where neighbors gather for hearty food, regional beer, and good company. Think part restaurant, part pub.

That is exactly the feel at Oppenheimer Gasthaus. Seating is limited by fire-marshal capacity, and the restaurant embraces European-style communal seating at long wooden tables. You may end up sharing a table with people you have never met, which the staff considers part of the charm.

The Gasthaus is also refreshingly unhurried. There is no table-turnover clock; once you are seated, the table is yours for as long as you like. Every dish is prepared from scratch, never pre-made or microwaved, so the restaurant is upfront that it is not the place for a quick bite. It is the place for a long, relaxed meal.

The menu is built around classic German comfort food, and prices are friendly: most sandwiches and sausage plates come in under $14, and schnitzel dinners start at $16.95. Highlights include:

Schnitzel, four ways — pork loin breaded and pan fried. Order it plain ($16.95), as Jagerschnitzel smothered in mushroom gravy ($17.95), Hungarian-style with a zesty sauce ($17.95), or as a Cordon Bleu stuffed with ham and Swiss ($24.95).

Rouladen ($22.95) — thinly sliced beef rolled around bacon, onions, mustard, and pickles.

Sauerbraten ($23.95) — beef marinated for three days in a sweet-and-sour sauce. It is served only on Sundays, so plan ahead. (Our favorite)

Kohlrouladen ($12.50) — two cabbage rolls with pork filling. The staff jokingly calls it "a German burrito."

Goulash over Spätzle ($12.75) — cubed beef chuck simmered in dark beer and spices over soft egg noodles.

Sausages — Currywurst in homemade curry sauce ($9.95), Weisswurst with a pretzel and house mustard ($13.50), a beer brat with sauerkraut on a roll ($8.95), and paprika-spiced Kilometer Sausage ($9.95).

Leberkase — the Bavarian meatloaf served warm on a Kaiser roll ($7.95), or as a Strammer Max on bread with ham and a sunny-side-up egg ($9.75).

Pork soup in a bread bowl ($11).

Starters include the customer-favorite Gurkensalat cucumber salad ($4.50), cheese spätzle ($6.95), and a large Bavarian pretzel ($12). Most entrées come with a choice of sides such as spätzle, sauerkraut, blue cabbage, German potato salad, lingonberries, Obatzda cheese spread, or pommes frites.

Desserts rotate, so ask your server what is available. Past offerings have included Kaesesahne, a light German cheese-cream cake. The restaurant has also shared the tradition of the Lebkuchenherz, the decorated gingerbread hearts sold at German festivals and given as tokens of affection.

The drink menu is one of the most extensive German selections in southern New Mexico. Weihenstephaner Hefe-Weissbier and Original Lager are on draft in half-liter ($7.50) and full-liter ($15) pours. Bottles include Paulaner Oktoberfest Märzen, Bitburger Pils, Warsteiner, Gaffel Kölsch, and Korbinian Doppelbock.

Wine lovers will find German Rieslings by the glass and bottle, including bottles from the celebrated Mosel producer J.J. Prüm, alongside Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Scheurebe, and Dornfelder.

Non-drinkers are covered too, with Bitburger Drive non-alcoholic beer and Spezi, the popular German cola-and-orange soda. Cocktails range from an Aperol Spritz and Hugo Spritz to a house creation called the Alamogordo Sunset.

After a big meal, staff recommend an old German remedy: a $3.50 shot of Underberg, a traditional herbal digestif that comes in a tiny paper-wrapped bottle.

The Gasthaus also enjoys sharing German drinking lore, including the history of the beer boot, or Bierstiefel.

Boot-shaped glass vessels date back in Europe to at least the 1600s, when glassblowers and guilds made them as decorative or ceremonial pieces. The most popular legend comes from World War I: a general promised his troops he would drink beer from his own leather boot if they won a battle. When they did, he kept his word. Glassmakers then began crafting glass boots so the victory toast could be repeated without ruining footwear.

No historical record ties the story to a specific general, battle, or date, so it is best enjoyed as folklore. Over the 20th century, the boot became a fixture of German and Austrian military and fraternity drinking culture. It doubles as a prank: tip it the wrong way and an air pocket in the toe releases a splash of beer onto the drinker's face. Hollywood comedies such as 2006's Beerfest later made the boot famous in America, and today it is a staple of Oktoberfest celebrations and beer halls worldwide.

First-time guests may notice a small light on their table. It is part of a traditional table-service system. Turn it on when you need your server, whether you want another drink, are ready to order, or are eyeing dessert, and the staff will come right over.

The system means no waving down servers and no interruptions asking whether everything is all right just as you take a bite. Guests set the pace of their own meal, which fits the Gasthaus philosophy. As the restaurant puts it: sit back, enjoy your schnitzel, and let the light do the talking.

Oppenheimer Gasthaus joins one of the most diverse dining lineups in the city. The Downtown MainStreet district covers the businesses and storefronts on New York Avenue and White Sands Boulevard from the 800 Block to the 1200 Block, and visitors can eat their way around the world without leaving it:

Independent shops and of course the Flickinger Theater, the Museum, the Zoo and Otero Arts are all within  walking distance and line the way, giving visitors plenty of reasons to linger before or after a meal.

Whether you are a schnitzel devotee or just curious about Kohlrouladen, Oppenheimer Gasthaus is worth a long, leisurely stop on your next trip downtown. As they say at the Gasthaus: Prost!

item.title: The Silver Fox Comes Home: Gary Hveem Remembered as Family at Tiger Stadium
item.description:
Former players and coaches from Gary Hveem's 10 Alamogordo teams gathered at Tiger Stadium to honor the coach who turned the program around. The current Tigers sent them home happy with a 48-7 win over Deming.

ALAMOGORDO — Thursday night lights belonged to Alamogordo, and for one evening they shone on a man who built much of what Tiger football still stands on.

Before the Alamogordo Tigers took the field against the Deming Wildcats, the school honored its senior football players, cheerleaders and the Gold Standard Athletic Trainers. Then, just before kickoff, the night turned to Coach Gary Hveem — "The Silver Fox" — who died Oct. 8 at age 86.

Twenty-eight players and coaches from Hveem's 10 Alamogordo teams came home to celebrate him. The reunion came together in less than three days.

The group posed for a team picture beneath the Tiger scoreboard. Then, as the Alamogordo Fighting Tigers headed into the tunnel, Hveem's former players and coaches followed them through it and onto Tiger Field.

They stopped short of the center logo — because, as every Tiger knows, you don't step on the Tiger. The current team formed a line and greeted each of Hveem's men one by one. A tribute to the coach rang out over the public address system as the alumni gathered for one more photo: "10 Years of Hveem."

The returning players were Deuce Sullivan, Michael J. Hopkin, Greg Lunsford, Tony Gonzalez, David Bailey, Dale Lindley, Billy Bagwell, Carlos Gutierres, Chris Sanchez, Chris Madril, Roger Romero, Jaime Rios, Jesus Macias, Mike Stringfield, Jimmy Gallardo, Doug Shoemaker, Steve Diehl, Bob Miller, Roger Black, Chris Rollerson, David Caraway and Herbert Delone. Coaches Robert Sepulveda, Joe Burton, Roger Sears and Art Lopez stood with them.

When Hveem arrived in 1976, the Alamogordo program was hurting. His predecessor had been let go after a 2-8 season, and the school picked a 35-year-old Iowan with a Norwegian name and hair already going gray — the source of the nickname that stuck for the rest of his life.

Hveem grew up on a farm in Osage, Iowa, served in the Navy and had gone 68-21-1 as a head coach at Iowa high schools. He was no stranger to New Mexico, having coached football and baseball at Eastern New Mexico in the early 1970s. He came to Alamogordo certified to teach physics, chemistry and biology, and he told his new players that past football experience wasn't required. That first fall, 20 boys who hadn't played the year before were on the roster.

The results came immediately. Alamogordo shut out El Paso Ysleta 7-0 in Hveem's first game, then beat Roswell and Goddard. At Artesia's Bulldog Bowl, the Tigers rallied from a 14-7 deficit with 37 seconds left, and quarterback Herb Delone — standing on Tiger Field again Thursday night — threw the two-point conversion that won it 15-14. Alamogordo climbed to No. 1 in the state's AAAA poll and finished 7-3, a stunning turnaround.

It was only the beginning. Over 10 seasons, Hveem's Tigers posted nine winning records and went 75-33-3. Twice they reached the AAAA state championship game, both times falling to Eric Roanhaus' Clovis Wildcats. His final team, in 1985, entered the title game 12-0 before losing 36-12.

Hveem never measured his work in wins and losses alone. After leaving the sideline, he spent a year with the New Mexico Activities Association, a decade as athletic director at Iowa City High School, and then another decade as the first athletic director in Rio Rancho Public Schools history, building that district's athletic program from scratch before retiring in 2007. Rio Rancho inducted him into its Hall of Honor in 2023.

His stated goal, at every stop, was to make athletics part of a student's whole education — a place for competition, integrity and honesty.

Robert "Bob" Sepulveda was one of the coaches who stood beside Hveem through the Tiger years, and he was there again Thursday at age 90, alongside fellow staff members Joe Burton, Roger Sears and Art Lopez. Vheem and Sepulveda remained lifelong friends and spoke as recently as a week before his death. 

The current Tigers made sure the evening ended the right way, dominating Deming 48-7.

Organizers thanked everyone who came out on short notice and said those who couldn't make it — because of travel or plans that couldn't be changed — were missed and in everyone's thoughts.

Hveem's family was close to the heart of the night: his wife, Fran — whom he had known since kindergarten and married in 1961 — and Jennifer Jennings, Josh, and Jacquelyn Hoover Hveem.

Photos above of the event were taken by Trisha Flores-Sullivan and Michele Trudeau Bagwell.

The silver hair turned white long before he retired. In Alamogordo, he will always be remembered as the Silver Fox of Tiger Stadium.

item.title: Commentary: Amendment 4 Writes a Paycheck Without a Job Description
item.description:
Vote NO on Constitutional Amendment 4. It sets a salary for New Mexico's 112 legislators but never defines the job that salary pays for.

Amendment 4 would pay each legislator the state's median household income — about $67,800 today — starting with members seated in January 2029. The figure adjusts every year after that. Legislators would keep their $247-a-day per diem, their mileage and their pension.

We understand the appeal. New Mexico is the only state that pays its lawmakers no salary, and serving in Santa Fe costs real money. But voters are being asked to approve the paycheck first and settle the work later. That is backwards.

The Legislature meets 60 days in odd-numbered years and 30 days in even-numbered years. Outside those sessions, nothing in Amendment 4 requires a minimum number of hours, a district office, town halls, constituent-service standards or attendance at interim committees.

The Legislative Council Service's own nonpartisan analysis notes the amendment leaves open what counts as legislative service, how the income figure is set, and how benefits, pensions and per diem are treated. It places no limit on outside income. No legislator would have to leave another job. A member could draw the full salary and keep a full-time career.

How much do legislators work now? Supporters cite a 2023 survey in which legislators reported averaging about 20 hours a week on legislative work year-round. Take that at face value: 20 hours times 52 weeks is about 1,040 hours — half a full-time schedule.

At $67,800, that is roughly $65 an hour, the equivalent of about $135,600 for a full-time worker. And that figure is self-reported, not drawn from time records. The Legislature's own 2022 study by UNM's Bureau of Business and Economic Research drew survey answers from 43 of the 112 members.

In a 60-day session year, salary plus session per diem alone comes to $82,620 — before interim committee days, mileage or pension credit. Add 20 interim committee days and it passes $87,500.

The pension is already generous. At today's per diem, 10 years of service earns about $31,100 a year for life; 20 years earns about $62,200. Lawmakers raised that formula by 50% in 2024.

On health care, current law lets legislators join the state plan only if they pay the full premium. But by deleting the constitutional ban on other allowances, Amendment 4 lets a future Legislature add benefits for itself.

The cost of salaries alone is about $7.6 million a year. The proposed pay would also exceed the 2025 national average legislative salary of $44,320, and top what lawmakers earn in Texas, Colorado and Arizona.

A nursing assistant working full time earns about $19 an hour. By supporters' own hours estimate, a legislator would earn about $65 an hour in salary alone.

These workers can be fired for not showing up. Amendment 4 sets no such standard for the people who would set their budgets.

Even some who favor pay have doubts about this version. The Rio Grande Foundation's Paul Gessing says he is not against salaries in principle, only this amount. An Albuquerque Journal opinion columnist who backs legislative pay plans to vote no because it arrives without transparency reforms.

A proposal worth supporting would:

Vote NO on Amendment 4, and ask every legislative candidate on your ballot to bring back a plan that defines the work before it sets the pay.

Voters should weigh the other side. Supporters — including Common Cause New Mexico, NM CAFé and the Vote For Change coalition — argue that an unpaid Legislature limits service to retirees, the wealthy and the self-employed.

Tying pay to median income keeps lawmakers' pay connected to ordinary families, and it falls if that income falls.

Per diem doesn't cover costs: most legislators surveyed said per diem and mileage fall short, and nine in ten said they work 30 or more days a year without claiming it.

A stronger Legislature: a UNM study ranked New Mexico near the bottom in legislative professionalism and recommended salaries, staff and longer sessions.

Voters are split: an August Journal Poll found 39% for the amendment, 21% against and 40% undecided or wanting details.

Our editorial board suggests a no vote on this amendment and a new amendment be introduced next legislative session better defining the terms and conditions with an independent citizens commission.
